Hansa had wanted to start a weekend pottery class for children for over a year. Her flat in Ahmedabad had a small balcony, and she only had Sundays free from her bank job.
She had three notebooks full of plans. Diagrams of where the wheels would go. Lists of clay suppliers. A rough budget. Lesson ideas for twelve weeks. Colour-coded timetables.
Every Sunday she sat with a notebook and added more. It felt like progress. Her friend Minakshi asked in March, "So when's the first class?"
"Soon. I'm still planning the lessons for weeks nine to twelve."
"Have you called the clay supplier?"
"Not yet."
By September, the notebooks were thicker. She still hadn't ordered clay, cleared the balcony or told a single parent.
One Sunday, flipping through all three, she felt a heavy sinking. It was a year of plans, and not one child had touched clay.

qa.q: How many notebooks of plans did Hansa have?
qa.a: She had three notebooks full of plans.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel flipping through the notebooks in September?
qa.a: She felt a heavy sinking, realising a year of planning had produced no class at all.

qa.q: What would you change first in Hansa's approach?
qa.a: Pick one concrete step, like calling the clay supplier this week, and do it before writing any more plans.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see Hansa's plans?
qa.a: Minakshi seems gently doubtful, asking when the first class is and whether the supplier has been called.

grounding: It shows a young professional filling notebooks with plans for a pottery class but never starting, since the writing feels like progress while the first step stays undone.

Jasleen's desk in her Noida flat was stacked with notebooks. One for the career switch into data work. One for the online course plan. One for the portfolio projects. Each had mind maps, lists and neat timetables in three pen colours.
Her flatmate Ankita picked one up. "This is beautiful. Which course did you enroll in?"
"None yet," Jasleen said. "I'm still comparing."
"It's been since Diwali."
"I know. But I want the plan to be right first."
That night Jasleen opened the newest notebook and started a fresh page: "Revised plan, version 6." She drew a timeline for the next six months.
Then she flipped back to version 1, from October. The first step was the same: sign up for the statistics course. It still wasn't done. Five versions of planning, and not one lesson watched.
She sat with the pen in her hand for a long time.

qa.q: What was the first step in version 1?
qa.a: Sign up for the statistics course.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt sitting with the pen in her hand?
qa.a: She probably felt stuck and uneasy, even a little ashamed, seeing five versions of planning with nothing started.

qa.q: What else could Jasleen do instead of writing version 7?
qa.a: She could sign up for the statistics course that same night, then plan only the next small step after it.

qa.q: How does Ankita see the notebooks?
qa.a: Ankita admires how beautiful they are but gently points out how long it has been without starting.

grounding: It shows a young professional who keeps writing plans without acting, so the notes feel like progress while the first real step stays undone.
